title: Role Specialization — Planner, Critic, Executor, Verifier

questions.question: A team needs one agent to design a plan and another to check whether the resulting artifact passes a test. Which separation helps?
options: Assign distinct roles with explicit outputs and checks
Let the executor approve its own output without testing
Replace the plan with a longer shared conversation
Give every agent the same prompt and ask for agreement
questions.explanation: Distinct roles define who plans, who executes, and who checks a concrete result; a verifier can test the artifact independently. Asking identical prompts for agreement leaves both agents exposed to the same mistaken assumptions.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between a critic and a verifier?
options: A verifier writes the plan; a critic executes code
A critic runs tests; a verifier judges style
A critic is subjective; a verifier runs deterministic checks
Both are identical LLM roles with different names
questions.explanation: A critic evaluates intent, quality, and plausibility; a verifier runs a deterministic test or schema check. Assigning test execution to the critic confuses subjective review with an objective pass/fail signal.

questions.question: An executor needs a detail that was omitted from the plan. What does ChatDev's communicative dehallucination pattern ask it to do?
options: Invent a likely value and keep the pipeline moving
Ask the verifier to change the user's specification
Ask the relevant role for the missing detail before continuing
Wait until the final paper is reviewed
questions.explanation: When required detail is missing, the executor should ask the role that owns the specification instead of inventing a value. A guessed detail can make downstream code internally consistent but still wrong for the user’s intent.

questions.question: The generated add function has the expected name, a def statement, and a return, but multiplies its inputs. Its critic checks only those surface features. Which role catches the behavior mismatch?
options: A deterministic verifier that runs the specified tests
A role router that chooses the next speaker
A critic that checks only for a def statement
A planner that only writes the function signature
questions.explanation: For the actual test (1, 2), the specified sum is 3; the buggy multiply returns 2 and fails the expected-value check. A critic that only looks for a definition, return, and matching name can miss this behavior mismatch.

questions.question: A pipeline has planner, executor, and critic roles, but every approval is based on an LLM saying the work looks good. What is missing?
options: More rounds of subjective approval
A second planner with the same prompt
A larger shared chat history for all roles over time
A code-based verifier with objective pass/fail checks
questions.explanation: A code-based verifier checks observable behavior—tests, types, or schema—rather than asking another LLM to approve similar prose. More rounds of subjective approval do not create an independent measurement.

questions.question: A critic requests a revision, but the executor cycles indefinitely between plausible changes. What limit does the lesson recommend?
options: Remove the verifier so revisions proceed faster
Cap revision rounds and escalate when the budget is exhausted
Let the critic run the executor's tools directly
Continue until the critic stops finding stylistic issues
questions.explanation: A small revision budget stops the critic-executor loop from consuming calls indefinitely; once it is exhausted, escalate or accept a defined fallback. Waiting for all stylistic concerns to disappear has no finite stopping condition.
